opus-5.5.text:
I think it's because AI research is the kind of work that compounds. If you have a system that can genuinely contribute to doing research on AI itself, then every improvement feeds back into the process of making the next improvement. That's a very different situation from a model that's just really good at answering questions or writing code on demand.

When I think about what research actually involves, it's not a single skill. You have to come up with a hypothesis, design an experiment that tests it, run it, notice when something looks off, debug it, and then decide what the result means and what to try next. A lot of that is long-horizon work. You might go days or weeks without a clean signal that you're on the right track. So building a model that can do that well forces you to solve many of the hard problems we care about anyway: reasoning over long time horizons, staying coherent across many steps, knowing when you're uncertain, and checking your own work.

Part of why I find it compelling is that we've seen models get remarkably good at well-defined problems, things like competition math or programming contests, where there's a clear question and a verifiable answer. Research is messier. Often the hardest part is figuring out what the right question even is. Getting from "can solve hard problems someone else posed" to "can pose and pursue good problems on its own" feels like the next real step.

And practically speaking, AI research is a domain we understand deeply. It's what we do every day, so we're well positioned to evaluate whether a model is actually helping or just producing something that looks plausible. That makes it a natural proving ground. If we can get models to be real collaborators there, I think a lot of what we learn carries over to science more broadly: biology, physics, materials, wherever progress is bottlenecked on people having time to run the next experiment.

So it's both a milestone in capability and an accelerant. That combination is why it feels like the thing to aim for.

r001.rationale: The response describes challenges in AI research and says progress can be bottlenecked by people’s time, but it does not identify limits of human intelligence as a constraint on AI research progress.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that the world’s demand for intelligence exceeds the supply humans can provide.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of it this way: so far, every big jump in AI capability has come from a loop where humans do the research and the models get better as a result. We run experiments, we look at what fails, we build better data, we improve the training recipe, and then we train again. That loop is bottlenecked on people. There are only so many researchers, and only so many ideas each of us can try in a year.

Something like the IMO result was interesting to me not mainly because of the math, but because it showed the model could sustain a long chain of reasoning on a hard, open-ended problem without anyone holding its hand. Research has a similar shape. You start with a vague question, you form a hypothesis, you try something, it doesn't work, you figure out why, and you adjust. If a model can do that reliably for math, it's not a crazy leap to think it can do that for the problems we face when we're trying to make the model itself better.

And once that happens, the thing that's been the bottleneck is no longer the bottleneck. The loop starts to close on itself. You can run many more experiments, explore many more ideas, and the rate of progress is no longer tied to how many people you can hire. That's why I see it as the milestone rather than one milestone among many. Most capabilities make the model more useful for some task. This one changes how fast we get all the others.

I'd add that it's also the point where we have to be most careful. If the loop is accelerating, you want to understand what's happening inside it, and you want humans to stay meaningfully in the driver's seat even if the day-to-day work is being done by models. So I think of it as both the most exciting milestone and the one where getting the details right matters the most.

r001.rationale: The response says AI research is bottlenecked by the limited number of human researchers and the number of ideas they can try, identifying human research capacity as a constraint on progress.

r002.rationale: It says models could enable more experiments and ideas, but does not state that the world’s demand for intelligence exceeds what humans can supply.

astra-6.text:
I think AI research is a particularly consequential capability because it can accelerate the process of making AI itself better. Today, progress depends on people coming up with ideas, running experiments, understanding what happened, and deciding what to try next. If AI can meaningfully contribute throughout that loop, then we can make progress faster.

And it’s a demanding test of what these systems can do. Research isn’t just answering a question where someone already knows the answer. It involves dealing with uncertainty, figuring out which questions matter, and sticking with a problem when the first few approaches don’t work.

That doesn’t mean the moment an AI can do research, everything suddenly takes off. Experiments still take compute and time, and promising ideas still need to be checked. But it would be a significant shift: AI would become a tool for improving the very technology that drives its capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could speed up research currently done by people, but does not identify limits of human intelligence as a constraint on AI research progress.

r002.rationale: It does not state that global demand for intelligence exceeds what humans can supply.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI research is a particularly important milestone because it can change the pace of progress in AI itself. So far, that progress has depended on people coming up with ideas, running experiments, understanding what happened, and deciding what to try next. If AI can help carry out that whole loop, then we could make progress much faster.

The key distinction is between a system that can solve a problem you’ve specified and a system that can figure out which problems are worth working on. Research requires dealing with uncertainty, noticing when an experiment challenges your assumptions, and finding a productive next step. That’s a much broader capability than answering a question correctly.

And if we can do that reliably, it could help us understand these systems better, too—how to evaluate them, how to make them more reliable, and how to keep human oversight effective as their capabilities grow.

r001.rationale: The response says AI progress has depended on people and could accelerate if AI carries out the research loop, but it does not identify limitations of human intelligence as a constraint.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that demand for intelligence exceeds what humans can supply.
